core: What a correlation is: a measure of how two variables move together (working definition attributed to the APA Dictionary of Psychology)
The three directions: positive (same direction), negative (opposite directions), zero/near-zero (no pattern), each with an original example
Strength: how tightly the pattern holds, stated simply, with the honest note that the number is a range (-1 to +1) and no invented statistics
Scatterplots as the picture of a correlation: one dot per data point, direction from the slope, strength from how tightly dots hug a line
What a correlation can and cannot show: links, not causes (the core boundary; the correlation-versus-causation deep dive is a sibling topic)
Uses: prediction and hypothesis generation, each named with one line
Honest framing: correlation is a clue, not a verdict
supporting: Variables as the things a correlation relates
Correlational research observes and measures variables as they occur, without manipulating them
A third variable can sit behind a correlation
outOfScope: Correlation versus causation in depth (sibling topic psychology:foundations:correlation-versus-causation)
The correlation coefficient's calculation, r-values, and statistical inference (owned by the statistics subject)

claims.claim: Correlation is a measure of the degree of a relationship between two variables — in plain words, how two variables move together.
A positive correlation means two variables move in the same direction: as one increases, the other tends to increase too, and as one decreases, the other tends to decrease.
A negative correlation means two variables move in opposite directions: an increase in one is associated with a decrease in the other, and vice versa.
When two variables show no consistent pattern of co-movement, the correlation is near zero (the variables are essentially unrelated); a negative correlation is not the same as no correlation.

The strength of a correlation is how tightly the pattern holds; when researchers put a number on a correlation it runs from -1 to +1, and the closer the number is to either end, the more strongly related — and more predictable — the variables are.

A scatterplot is the picture of a correlation: each dot is one data point carrying two pieces of information (its value on each variable), and the stronger the correlation, the closer the dots fall to a straight line.
Correlation shows links between variables, not causes: establishing that a relationship exists tells little about cause and effect, because other factors may be involved.
Correlations have predictive value: when two variables move together, knowing one helps anticipate the other.
A correlation can generate hypotheses: a discovered pattern leaves several possible explanations open, and each becomes a question researchers can test with other methods.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The casual phrase 'correlation implies causation' versus the standard position that correlation alone never establishes cause.
positions: Popular usage often treats a measured link as proof that one thing causes the other (e.g., a news headline claiming a study 'shows' screen time delays sleep from a correlational app dataset).
OpenStax Psychology 2e and the Noba Project state the standard position: a correlation between variables does not imply cause and effect, and a third variable may drive both.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the standard position and holds the boundary lightly: this topic covers what correlation is and does; the full correlation-versus-causation treatment is its own sibling topic (psychology:foundations:correlation-versus-causation).

sourceRecords.title: Research Designs
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read live 2026-08-22. Supports: correlational research passively observes and measures variables without intervening and usually cannot infer what causes what; a scatterplot plots the relation between two scores, each dot a data point carrying two pieces of information; a positive correlation means the two variables go up or down together (dots extend from bottom left to upper right); a negative correlation means they move in opposite directions; the strength of a correlation is how well the two variables align; a weak correlation corresponds some of the time but not most; variables so weakly related as to be unrelated are uncorrelated, with values zero or very close to zero; from a correlation alone several explanations are possible (a third variable may cause both), which is why correlation does not mean causation.
